newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK trade deficit narrows, but exports growth slows.
newsitem.headline: HK trade deficit narrows, but exports growth slows.

text.p: Hong Kong's trade deficit narrowed in September compared with the previous month, but analysts said there was little reason to cheer in view of a slow-down in exports growth.

The provisional visible trade deficit stood at HK$4.6 billion in September, versus HK$7.21 billion in August and HK$4.33 billion in September 1995, the Census and Statistics Department said on Tuesday.
The latest figure, equivalent to 3.5 percent of the value of imports, was the lowest trade deficit recorded in a single month since October 1995.
Total exports, comprising re-exports and domestic exports, fell 0.4 percent year-on-year to HK$126.1 billion in September.
That compared with a growth rate of 3.1 percent in August.

Re-exports rose 2.2 percent to HK$107.8 billion in September, while domestic exports were down 14 percent to HK$18.3 billion. In August, re-exports grew 6.1 percent and domestic exports fell 11.4 percent.
Imports dipped 0.2 percent over a year earlier to $130.7 billion in September. That compared with a 0.7 percent rise in August.
K.K. Chan, chief economist at Nomura Research Institute, pointed out that Hong Kong's September growth figures were poorer than those in August.

"Exports still continued to decline and to some regard that was a little bit of a surprise, given the fact that China's exports have started to perform better over the third quarter," said Arthur Woo, assistant economist at NatWest Markets.

China's exports increased eight percent year-on-year in September, picking up steam after a sluggish performance for most of 1996. Hong Kong is a major entrepot for imports and exports to and from China.
Joanne Yim , manager of economic research at Hang Seng Bank, said the poor performance in exports could have been due to the strong U.S. dollar, to which the Hong Kong dollar is pegged.
"Also, recovery in western European countries and Japan has not been as fast as expected," she said.

"The trade deficit fell mainly because imports fell. The fall had been expected because when our consumer spending was not so strong," she said. "Also at this stage of the airport project, we didn't need to import much machinery."
The territory is building a new airport scheduled to be operational in 1998. The development and related projects have necessitated considerable imports of machinery.
Woo said the fall in imports also reflected economic activity in the third quarter "was still quite subdued".
Analysts were split on the trade outlook in coming months.
"The fourth quarter is expected to be much better than the third quarter," said Chan. Improving China trade would help.
Woo agreed. "I would probably see exports to pick up over the fourth quarter...I would generally expect the trade deficit to narrow over the coming months," he said.
But the September figures reinforced his belief the 4.7 percent economic growth forecast for 1996 could not be achieved, Woo said.
Yim, however, did not expect much improvement in exports. "We expect exports to continue to be poor in coming months, because orders-on-hand have been poor," she said.
August orders-on-hand fell nine percent in value on the year against a seven percent drop in July.
U.S. customers might grow more cautious with Hong Kong as Washington was tightening up enforcement of rules on the country-of-origin of imports into its territory.
